text: Three questions, as old as the world.
Who makes it? Who keeps it? And who, in the end, lets it go?
The first answer is Brahma, the creator, born on a lotus, with four faces that look out in four directions.
From him came the Vedas, the oldest sacred knowledge, and from his thought, the world itself.
A single day of Brahma lasts four billion, three hundred and twenty million years.
asr: A single day of Brahma lasts 4 billion, 320 million years.

text: The second answer is Vishnu, the preserver, at rest on the coils of the serpent Shesha, on the ocean between the worlds.
asr: The second answer is Vishnu, the preserver, at rest on the coils of the serpent Shasha, on the ocean between the worlds.

text: Whenever the world falls out of balance, he returns, in a new form for each age.
A fish.
A great tortoise.
A wild boar.
Half man, half lion.
A dwarf.
A warrior.
A prince.
A cowherd.
A teacher.
And a horseman, still to come.
The third answer is Shiva, the destroyer, the ascetic of Mount Kailash, who caught the falling river Gunga in his hair.
asr: The third answer is Shiva, the destroyer, the ascetic of Mount Kailash, who caught the falling river Gungo in his hair.

text: His dance keeps the rhythm of the cosmos: in one hand, the drum of creation; in another, the fire that ends it.
Four ages turn, each shorter and darker than the last. At the end of the last, he dances the world away.
Creator, preserver, destroyer. Not three gods apart, but three faces of one reality.
The Tri-moor-tee. And when the last page is turned, the first is painted again.
asr: The Trimurti. And when the last page is turned, the first is painted again.
